title: Some People Avoid You Because They Owe You an Apology
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece explores why team members sometimes avoid a leader after an embarrassing incident: they owe an apology and find the power dynamic makes offering one feel especially exposing. It argues that self-secure leaders neither require nor demand apologies, but must still actively address the resulting awkwardness since avoidance disrupts the open communication leadership depends on. The recommended move is for the leader to proactively signal that the issue is already forgotten, removing the pressure that keeps the other person distant. It closes by framing this as an act of quiet maturity that prioritizes team function over personal vindication.
points: Explains why owing an apology to a leader intensifies avoidance behavior
Argues self-secure leaders don't require or demand apologies from others
Recommends leaders proactively signal an issue is already forgotten
Frames the practice as prioritizing team function over personal vindication
quotes: There are a truckload of reasons people avoid leaders at times.
Saving face by avoiding the people involved after an embarrassing or regrettable incident is normal behavior.
Acknowledging to anyone with higher status that you have committed an error worthy of an apology exposes the power relationship in a raw way.
Leaders who are self-secure and understand the complex nature of relationships neither require nor demand apologies.
The best leaders go out of their way to tell those who owe them an apology that everything is good and the incident is already behind them.
For mature leaders, what is best for the team far outweighs the need for personal satisfaction when it comes to receiving an apology.
